title: Building Actions
summary: Write functions with multiple steps inside them — and see how the order of lines matters.

content.title: Multiple Lines Inside a Function
content.summary: Every indented line inside the function runs in order, top to bottom, each time you call it.
content.body: A function can do as many things as you like. Every indented line is part of it:
content.codeBlock:
def open_treasure():
    print("The chest creaks open...")
    print("A golden light spills out.")
    print("You found 50 gold!")

open_treasure()
content.note: Python runs all three `print` lines in order, every time you call `open_treasure()`.

content.title: Order Matters
content.summary: Lines inside a function run top to bottom, just like normal code — sequence is everything.
content.body: The lines inside a function run in the exact order you write them:
content.codeBlock:
def enter_shop():
    print("A bell jingles as you enter.")
    print("The shopkeeper looks up.")
    print("What would you like to buy?")
content.note: If you swapped the last two lines, the shopkeeper would speak before looking up. Order tells the story.

content.title: Where Does the Function End?
content.summary: The function ends when indentation goes back to the left margin.
content.body: Python knows the function is finished when the indent stops:
content.codeBlock:
def battle():
    print("The enemy charges!")   # inside the function
    print("You dodge!")            # inside the function

print("Battle over.")              # outside the function (no indent)
content.note: The last `print` runs once, after any calls to `battle()`.

content.title: Using Variables Inside Functions
content.summary: You can use variables inside a function body just like anywhere else.
content.body: Functions can create and use their own variables:
content.codeBlock:
def show_score():
    score = 100
    print("Current score:", score)

show_score()
content.note: The variable `score` exists while the function runs. Each call to `show_score()` starts fresh.

content.title: Errors You Might See
content.summary: Three common function errors — and how to spot them.
content.body:
Functions add a few new error types to watch for:

• `NameError` — you called a function (like `jump()`) before defining it, or you misspelled the name.
• `IndentationError` — the lines inside `def` need to be indented 4 spaces.
• `SyntaxError` — usually a missing `:` after `def name():` or a missing `()` on the function name.

If Python complains, read the line number it gives you. The fix is almost always small.

steps.instruction: Step 1: Replace the `pass` inside `open_treasure()` with 2–3 indented `print()` lines describing finding treasure (you found a chest, what's inside, what happens). Run the code — nothing should appear yet, because no one has *called* the function.
Step 2: At the bottom (no indent — outside the functions), add the call `open_treasure()`. Run it. Your treasure lines should print.
Step 3: Now fill in `game_over()` with 2 indented `print()` lines — something like a goodbye message. Run it. Nothing new should appear yet — `game_over()` isn't being called.
Step 4: Add `game_over()` after `open_treasure()` at the bottom. Run it. You should see all your treasure lines, **then** the game-over lines, in order.

bonusSteps.instruction: Bonus: Add a third function called `level_up()` that prints a short celebration. Then call them in this order at the bottom: `open_treasure()`, `level_up()`, `game_over()`.

progressiveHints: Replace each `pass` with 2–3 indented `print()` lines describing that moment.
Make sure every line inside the function is indented 4 spaces.
After both definitions, write `open_treasure()` and `game_over()` to call them.

Answer shape:
def open_treasure():
    print("You found a chest!")
    print("Inside: a magic sword.")

def game_over():
    print("Game over.")
    print("Thanks for playing!")

open_treasure()
game_over()
